title: JSON and Web APIs
summary: JSON stores data as text. An API is a set of rules that lets one program ask another program for data.
introduction: JSON stores data as text. An API is a set of rules that lets one program ask another program for data. Think of asking for a book list at a library desk. Read a small JSON answer first, then see how a program asks for one.
learningObjectives: Convert Python data to JSON text and back with dumps() and loads()
Explain how JSON types map to Python types and what cannot be serialised
Save and load JSON files with dump() and load()
Call a web API with urllib.request and handle HTTP and network errors

blocks.text: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is plain text: objects in braces, arrays in brackets, strings in double quotes, numbers, `true`, `false` and `null`. Python has a matching type for each, which is why the conversion is nearly free.

rows: `list` (tuples are written as arrays and come back as lists)

blocks.title: convert.py
blocks.code:
import json

user = {"name": "Ada", "age": 36, "languages": ["Python", "SQL"], "admin": False, "manager": None}

text = json.dumps(user)
print(text)
print(type(text).__name__)

data = json.loads(text)
print(data["languages"][1], data["manager"])
print(data == user)

print(json.loads('{"total": 3, "items": [1, 2.5, "three"]}'))

blocks.title: python convert.py

blocks.text: `dumps` (dump to string) serialises Python data into JSON text; `loads` (load from string) parses JSON text back into Python data. The round trip is faithful for the types in the table, so `data == user` is `True`. Notice the spelling changes: `False` becomes `false`, `None` becomes `null` and every string gets double quotes, because that is what JSON requires.
Pretty printing and what cannot be serialised

blocks.title: pretty.py
python pretty.py

blocks.text: `indent` adds line breaks and indentation for human readers, and `sort_keys` makes the output stable, which keeps version-control diffs small. Dates, sets and your own objects have no JSON equivalent and raise `TypeError`; convert them first (`isoformat()` for dates, `list()` for sets, a dictionary for objects) or pass a `default=` function that does the conversion.

blocks.title: settings.py
blocks.code:
import json

settings = {"theme": "dark", "font_size": 14, "recent": ["notes.txt", "todo.md"]}

with open("settings.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    json.dump(settings, file, indent=2)

with open("settings.json", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    loaded = json.load(file)

print(loaded["font_size"] + 2)
print(loaded["recent"][0])
print(loaded == settings)

blocks.title: load() and loads() are not interchangeable
blocks.text: `json.load("settings.json")` fails with `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'read'`, because `load()` wants an open *file object*, not a path, while `loads()` wants a *string* of JSON. Passing a file object to `loads()` fails too, with `TypeError: the JSON object must be str, bytes or bytearray, not TextIOWrapper`. Remember the `s`: `dumps` and `loads` work with strings, `dump` and `load` work with files.

A web API is a URL that returns JSON instead of a page. The standard library's `urllib.request` can fetch it, and `json.load()` reads straight from the response object. The examples use JSONPlaceholder, a free fake API for testing that always returns the same sample data, so your output will match as long as you are online.

blocks.title: api.py
blocks.code:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen

with urlopen("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1", timeout=10) as response:
    print(response.status, response.headers["Content-Type"])
    user = json.load(response)

print(user["name"])
print(user["email"])
print(user["address"]["city"])
print(sorted(user.keys()))

blocks.title: python api.py
blocks.content:
200 application/json; charset=utf-8
Leanne Graham
Sincere@april.biz
Gwenborough
['address', 'company', 'email', 'id', 'name', 'phone', 'username', 'website']

blocks.text: The response is an object you use inside a `with` block, just like a file. `status` is the HTTP status code (200 means success), the headers tell you the content type, and `json.load(response)` parses the body. From then on `user` is a plain dictionary, navigated exactly as in [Dictionaries](/tutorials/python/dictionaries).

blocks.title: post.py
blocks.code:
import json
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

payload = json.dumps({"title": "Learn Python", "completed": False, "userId": 1}).encode("utf-8")
request = Request(
    "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos",
    data=payload,
    headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
    method="POST",
)
with urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
    print(response.status)
    created = json.load(response)
print(created)

blocks.text: To send data, build a `Request` with a body (bytes, hence `.encode("utf-8")`), the content type header and the HTTP method. The fake API answers `201 Created` and echoes the record with a new `id`; a real API would store it. The same pattern covers `PUT` and `DELETE`.

blocks.title: fetch.py
python fetch.py
blocks.content:
{'userId': 1, 'id': 1, 'title': 'delectus aut autem', 'completed': False}
HTTP error: 404 Not Found
None
Network error: could not reach the server
None

blocks.text: `HTTPError` means the server answered with an error status (404 not found, 401 unauthorised, 500 server error); `URLError` means no usable answer at all (no network, unknown host, timeout). `HTTPError` is a subclass of `URLError`, so it must be listed first. Always pass a `timeout`, otherwise a silent server can hang your program forever. The `.invalid` domain is reserved and never resolves, which makes it handy for testing the failure path.

blocks.title: requests and real projects
blocks.text: Most Python code uses the third-party `requests` library, where the first example shrinks to `requests.get(url, timeout=10).json()`. Installing it is the first thing you do in [Virtual Environments and pip](/tutorials/python/virtual-environments). Designing your own API is covered in [REST API](/tutorials/rest-api) and [FastAPI](/tutorials/fastapi).

questions.question: `json.___(text)` parses a string of JSON into Python data.
questions.explanation: `loads` reads from a string (the `s`), `load` reads from an open file object, and `dumps`/`dump` go the other way.

questions.question: What does Python's `None` become when serialised to JSON?
questions.explanation: JSON has `null` for the absence of a value; `None` maps to it and comes back as `None`.
